title: Cleaning and dressing a wound
asks: how do I clean a wound
clean a cut in the field
how to wash out a dirty wound
what do I use to clean a gash
do I pour alcohol or iodine on a wound
how much water to rinse a wound
cut myself with a knife how to clean and cover it
cleaning a woond with creek water
no bandages what can I use for a dressing
should I close a dirty cut with tape or stitches
answer: Stop the bleeding first. If a bandage was put on to control bleeding, do not remove it: seek medical care.
Seek medical care for: a large cut that may need closing, any suspected damage to nerves, vessels or muscles, an object impaled in the wound, and all animal bites.
Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water before handling the wound or dressings.
Clean the skin around the wound thoroughly with soap and water.
Clean blood clots, dirt and visible foreign material out of the wound.
Wash the wound out thoroughly by flushing it with at least 1 litre of clean water, and use the whole litre. A small wound can be washed with soap and drinkable water.
Use clean, drinkable water. If the water is not drinkable, boil it for a minimum of 3 minutes and cool it to body temperature first.

Put the water under pressure: poke a small hole in a clean bottle and squeeze the bottle, or use a syringe. For a large wound, water can be poured onto the wound from any large container while gently scrubbing.
Use more water for bigger or dirtier wounds: 1 to 3 litres for small or clean wounds, 4 to 8 litres for intermediate or dirty wounds, 9 litres or more for large or very dirty wounds.

Dress the wound with sterile gauze if available. If there are no sterile supplies, use clean sheets, towels or clothing, dry and not visibly soiled. Use a pressure dressing if the wound is still bleeding.
Keep the dressing clean and dry. Inspect it at least every 24 hours and replace it when it is soiled.
warnings: An object impaled in the wound: do not move it. Tell the person to remain still, surround the object with several layers of bulky dressings built up around it, and seek medical assistance.
Never close a dirty or infected wound, or a deep wound that continues to bleed inside.
If you cannot wash the wound out because dressings are limited, leave the original dressing in place and reinforce it.
Rinse water: the JTS wound-care guideline, in its notes on irrigating (rinsing out) wounds, says additives such as iodine, bacitracin or alcohol are not associated with reduced infection.
Do not use very high pressure: it is not associated with reduced infection and has been associated with tissue damage and driving bacteria deeper into the tissues.
A tetanus vaccination is needed if the person is not vaccinated or not up to date.
All animal bites need medical evaluation, especially those from unfamiliar or wild animals, deep bite wounds, or bites that become red, swollen or increasingly painful.

quotes.text: In general, if the bandaging was applied to control bleeding, do not remove. Seek medical care.
A large laceration may require suturing. Medical care should be sought if damage to nerves, vessels, or muscles is suspected.

When handling dressings, thorough washing of hands with soap and water is extremely important. If at all possible, use sterile gloves when handling wounds and removing or reapplying new dressings. Use of sterile gauze is recommended. However, if sterile supplies are not available, use clean sheets, towels, or clothing torn into 2" or 3" strips.

Haemorrhage control: stop bleeding as above. • Prevent infection: –– Clean wound of blood clots, dirt, dead or dying tissue, foreign bodies. –– Clean skin around the wound thoroughly with soap and water or antiseptic. –– Thoroughly wash out wound by flushing with at least 1 litre of clean water. The water should be under pressure to thoroughly clean the wound. To create a high pressure stream, use a syringe (with 14 g needle or IV catheter attached) or poke a small hole in a clean bottle and squeeze the bottle. Be sure to use the entire litre. –– If not vaccinated or not up to date, give tetanus vaccination. • Dressing wounds: –– Dress wound with sterile gauze if available. –– Use a pressure dressing if the wound is still bleeding.
Thoroughly cleanse wound with sterile saline solution, or clean water. Be sure and remove all visible dirt and foreign material. Place sterile gauze on the wound.

Better: Irrigate wounds with clean, potable tap water. Minimum: Irrigate wounds with the cleanest water available (nonpotable water should be boiled for a minimum of 3 minutes and then cooled to body temperature).

Evaluate the wound size and contamination level to determine the optimal amount of irrigation: 1–3L for small or clean wounds, 4–8L for intermediate or dirty wounds, and ≥9L for large or very dirty wounds.
Additives such as iodine, bacitracin, or alcohol are not associated with reduced infection.
Very high-pressure (>15 psi) irrigation is not associated with reduced infection and has been associated with tissue damage and injection of bacteria deeper into the tissues.

For moderate sized wounds, a bulb syringe or bottle with puncture holes in the top can be used for low pressure (<6 psi) irrigation. For large wounds, bags of IV fluids can be connected to IV tubing to facilitate large-volume irrigation or any large container may be used to pour water onto the wound while gently scrubbing the wound.
Wash smaller wounds with soap and potable water. Keep dressings clean and dry. Change soiled dressings as needed.
If packaged medical dressings are not available, a clean piece of cloth may be used. If used as an alternate, the cloth should not be visibly soiled and should be dry.

Minimum: Wash smaller wounds with soap, if available, and potable water. Irrigate larger wounds with potable water (cooled before use if boiled) and pour across the wound. If unable to irrigate because dressings are limited, leave the original dressing and reinforce/secure it.
Better: Inspect dressing at least every 24 hours and change as needed. Remove and replace soiled dressings at least every 24 hours.
At no time should dirty or infected wounds be closed. Wounds that continue to bleed inside, particularly if deep, should not be closed either.

Apply first aid for an impaled object as follows: • Tell the casualty to remain still and not to move the impaled object. • Expose the injury by cutting away or removing the clothing or equipment around the wound site.
Place several layers of bulky dressings around the injury site so that the dressings surround the object. • Use additional bulky materials or dressings to build up the area around the object.
Immobilize the affected area with a splint or sling, if applicable. • Check for a pulse distal (far side of the wound) to the injury site. • Treat for shock, if necessary. • Seek medical assistance.

Seek medical attention. It is important to seek medical evaluation for all animal bites, especially those from unfamiliar or wild animals, deep wounds, or those that become red, swollen, or increasingly painful.

conflict: OBJECTS IN THE WOUND: ATP 4-02.11 (2026) para 14-23 says do not move an impaled object, build dressings around it and seek medical assistance (only an object through the cheek with both ends visible is removed); HHS Ship's Medicine Chest 2003 says foreign objects protruding from a puncture wound that are easily grasped should be removed with sterile tweezers if removal will not further damage tissues (objects in the skull or brain are left in place); WHO-ICRC BEC 2018 and Ship's Medicine Chest say clean the wound of dirt and foreign bodies. The card removes only dirt and visible loose material and leaves impaled objects. ANTISEPTIC ON THE WOUND (the card recommends none; the JTS line was relabelled 2026-11-25 after the reviewer's note on the animal-bite card): the JTS Wound Management PFC 2017 sentence 'Additives such as iodine, bacitracin, or alcohol are not associated with reduced infection' stands under that guideline's 'Irrigation notes', between its Dakin's solution recipe and its note on irrigation pressure, so it is about what is added to the rinse fluid, not about an antiseptic put on a wound after cleaning. The warning used to give the sentence with no label, which read as a statement about antiseptics in general; it now says it is the JTS guideline's note on rinsing. The label comes from the heading; heading and sentence are on different pages of the PDF, so the quote holds the sentence only. On antiseptic after cleaning the kit says: ATP 4-02.11 bite care para 16-5, after cleaning apply an antiseptic solution or ointment; WHO-ICRC BEC, clean the skin around the wound with soap and water or antiseptic; Ship's Medicine Chest, if antiseptics are used pick one not harmful to tissue (1% silvedene, bacitracin, neosporin). The card still gives no line on antiseptic applied after cleaning, so the ask 'do I pour alcohol or iodine on a wound' is answered only as far as the JTS rinse note goes; reviewer and owner to decide whether an attributed line (ATP 4-02.11 or the Ship's Medicine Chest) should be added. REMOVING A DRESSING: Ship's Medicine Chest says do not remove bandaging applied to control bleeding and seek medical care; ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says do not remove a pressure dressing even when blood soaked, leave it 1 or 2 days, then change daily; JTS Nursing Interventions 2025 and Ship's Medicine Chest say change dressings daily or at least every 24 hours. BOILING TIME for rinse water: JTS Wound Management says boil nonpotable water a minimum of 3 minutes; the kit's EPA drinking-water guidance says 1 minute (3 minutes above 5,000 feet). PRESSURE: WHO BEC says use a high pressure stream (syringe, or squeezed bottle with a small hole); JTS says a bottle with puncture holes gives low pressure (<6 psi), a syringe with catheter gives the ideal 6–15 psi, and very high pressure (>15 psi) is harmful. PUNCTURE WOUNDS: Ship's Medicine Chest says bleeding from a puncture wound is encouraged to flush out foreign material; no other source says this. FEMA P-2064 (2020) has no wound care.

review.notes: previous review: (verdict pass, by claude-opus-5-5 (xhigh), independent review 2026-11-24) Confirmed in context: HHS (do not remove bleeding-control bandaging; when to seek care; hand washing; clean cloth strips; cleanse and remove visible dirt; never close dirty or infected or deep bleeding wounds), WHO BEC (clean clots and debris, skin with soap, at least 1 litre under pressure, tetanus, sterile gauze, pressure dressing), JTS Wound Management 2017 (potable water, boil non-potable 3 min and cool, 1-3/4-8/9+ litres, additives not helpful, very high pressure harmful, bottle or pouring for large wounds), JTS Nursing 2025 (soap and water for small wounds, clean dry cloth, inspect/replace every 24 h, reinforce if dressings are short), ATP 4-02.11 (impaled object; animal bites). Bleeding control is first. Object, antiseptic, dressing-change, boil-time, pressure and puncture-wound disagreements are all listed. No PDF junk. Minor: A6 'at least 1 litre' and A9 '1 to 3 litres for small or clean wounds' agree; fine.
